text: We propose Sparse Routing Adapters (SRA), a parameter-efficient method for adapting multilingual translation models to low-resource language pairs.
On WMT14 En-De and two low-resource pairs, SRA improves BLEU over LoRA while training 40% fewer parameters.
SRA achieves state-of-the-art results on the FLORES-200 Nepali-English benchmark.
Adapting large translation models to new language pairs remains costly.
Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA reduce this cost but treat all layers uniformly.
We hypothesize that routing updates to a sparse subset of layers is sufficient for low-resource adaptation.
SRA learns a gating score for each layer and updates only the top-k layers.
We set k to 4 in all experiments.
We evaluate on WMT14 En-De, FLORES-200 Nepali-English, and FLORES-200 Sinhala-English.
We compare against full fine-tuning, LoRA, and prefix tuning.
We report BLEU and chrF on the official test sets.
All results are averaged over three random seeds.
Models are trained on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU for at most 12 hours.
Table 1: BLEU and chrF on three language pairs (mean of three seeds).
SRA outperforms LoRA by 1.2 BLEU on En-De and by 2.1 BLEU on Nepali-English.
On Sinhala-English, SRA and LoRA perform comparably (within 0.3 BLEU).
On Nepali-English, SRA reaches 18.4 BLEU, the highest score reported on this benchmark to our knowledge.
SRA trains 40% fewer parameters than LoRA.
Most selected layers lie in the upper half of the decoder.
This suggests that low-resource adaptation mainly changes output-side representations.
We only evaluate on three language pairs, and our results may not transfer to other scripts.
We did not compare against recent adapter-merging methods.
SRA offers a simple way to adapt translation models with fewer trainable parameters.
This position paper discusses how code generation benchmarks are constructed and reported.
Code generation benchmarks have grown rapidly in number.
Many benchmarks reuse problems from public programming sites.
Reusing public problems raises the risk that test items appear in training data.
Reporting practices also differ in how many samples are drawn per problem.
We list questions that benchmark authors may consider when releasing a dataset.
We introduce a curriculum sampling strategy for graph contrastive learning.
Our strategy improves node classification accuracy on Cora and PubMed.
Negative samples are ordered from easy to hard during training.
We use a two-layer GCN encoder for all methods.
Accuracy on Cora increases from 82.1% to 83.0%.
